#10501. AMD shares how it can retain 95% of server performance with just half the DRAM, sidestepping memory shortages with MEXT

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

MEXT offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and serves them up with a predictive AI model.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In June, AMD overtook the predictive memory engine known as MEXT, which claims to offer upwards of 99% of the performance of a system with full DRAM capacity while running with as little as 25% of the physical DIMMs. The technology offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and uses an AI model to serve pages before they’re needed, and AMD says it plans to extend the tech across a wide swath of its IT infrastructure next year.

The pitch behind MEXT seems too good to be true. According to AMD and MEXT founder Gary Smerdon, the technology can cut the physical DRAM required in a server by 20% to 75% depending on the application and performance target. That missing memory still registers as installed DRAM to the OS. Instead of DRAM, however, MEXT uses relatively inexpensive flash storage to offload cold pages, flying them back in as they’re needed with an AI model. In some of AMD’s internal workloads, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, the company says it’s able to achieve 95% of the performance of a full server while running at 50% DRAM capacity with MEXT.

AMD has deployed MEXT internally on 145 servers, which it says will expand to 2,000 servers next year. In addition, the company has announced a partnership with HPE to bring MEXT to customers. Currently, we’re in phase 1 of the rollout, with some EPYC Venice servers carrying a “MEXT Ready” badge and a dedicated NVMe drive or bay for the offload. Phase 2 brings MEXT licenses out to these servers, as well as the RAM View application. AMD hasn’t said when Phase 2 will begin.

The AI-driven DRAM pricing surge impacts more than just gaming PCs, with enterprises also feeling the brunt of price increases, even if they aren’t running AI workloads. If MEXT is able to achieve what AMD claims, it could be transformative given the current market. Because of that, it’s worth understanding what exactly MEXT is, as well as what AMD claims it can do.

Although MEXT is exciting in concept, it’s obvious that AMD is taking a conservative approach to the rollout. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, after all. The applications of MEXT are currently narrow, though AMD says it’s expanding the workloads it’s using MEXT on with promising early results.

The basic setup of MEXT is simple in concept: cold pages go to flash, AI brings those pages back as needed, and it’s as if the memory was never missing in the first place. The main problem should be obvious. Flash is orders of magnitude slower than DRAM, so streaming pages back into memory from flash as they’re needed isn’t feasible. MEXT’s trick is using an AI model to predict the pages you’ll need. And, as long as the model is able to stay ahead by at least the transfer latency from the SSD, it’s as if the physical DRAM was installed the whole time.

This isn’t a crazy concept considering how a transformer-based LLM, which MEXT uses, operates. If you’re unfamiliar with the inner workings, this open-source visualization breaks down the concept of a transformer AI model cleanly. The foundational concept is next token prediction, which underpins the design of modern LLMs. Given a set of tokens, the LLM determines which token (word, portion of a word, etc.) is most likely to come next. It makes a prediction. In the case of MEXT, it’s predicting what page is needed next, not what word comes next.

Memory offloading to flash isn’t a new concept, but MEXT founder Gary Smerdon says that AI is the critical difference in this technology. MEXT itself is deployed as a Linux kernel module that works with any Linux distro. It uses an “ensemble of AI models,” with the primary transformer-based LLM driving the technology. And critically, it doesn’t come pre-trained.

Instead, AMD says that MEXT trains in under a second when first deployed, operates on one EPYC core without a GPU, and continually trains as the workload progresses. This approach makes sense given the varied workloads that MEXT may apply to. The idea is that it would learn the access patterns of the application in order to drive that prediction engine.

MEXT isn’t perfect, but it doesn’t need to be perfect in every situation. For instance, the order of stored pages isn’t important. With text, an LLM needs to predict the correct text in the correct order, but with MEXT, the order doesn’t matter. As long as the page is in DRAM when it’s needed, that’s fine.

In order to understand the application of MEXT to different workloads, AMD has developed RAM View to go alongside the tech. It’s a memory utilization tool that shows which pages are hot and which have gone cold. As you can see from the example above, a system with 1.5 TB of memory shows near-full utilization across the full workload, but around half of the pages stored in memory haven’t been touched in five minutes or more at any given time.

AMD provided this generalized example and didn’t clarify what workload it was testing. That’s very important, as the utilization breakdown will look vastly different depending on the application(s) running on the server. Initially, AMD is applying MEXT to critical EDA applications it uses internally, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, but the company says it has focused on optimizing agentic AI, database, and media and entertainment workloads as well.

This is important not only because memory access patterns change between applications, but also because performance in those applications reacts differently when a system doesn’t have enough memory. The “memory wall,” as AMD calls it, should be a familiar concept regardless of whether you’ve ever touched a server. With MEXT, AMD says it’s trying to extend this memory wall, which may look different for different applications.

For instance, the company is confident that many workloads can reduce capacity by around 20% to 25%. As the reduction increases, however, the applications become more specialized, and the performance delta becomes greater.

AMD has shared some internal MEXT results, which look impressive, though as usual, it’s always smart to handle first-party benchmarks like this with skepticism. Starting with PrimeTime, where AMD has focused much of its attention on MEXT up to this point, it says servers running at 50% capacity retain 95% of the performance of a full server, and going down to as little as 25% capacity still maintains 80% of the application’s performance.

PrimeTime demands a lot of memory for large designs. There are some applications where performance is nearly identical, according to AMD. In a 3-node cluster running in Azure with 5th-gen EPYC CPUs, AMD says MEXT offers 99% of the performance of the full cluster while running at 50% DRAM capacity with the Spark SQL workload from the TPC-DS benchmark. SQL databases try to cache as much data as possible in memory to prevent I/O bottlenecks, creating a golden opportunity for tech like MEXT that wants to free cold pages.

Perhaps the most applicable workload at the current moment, however, is agentic AI, and AMD says MEXT has similar applications there. Across a five-agent concurrent geomean, AMD claims 99% of the performance of a full server with 50% memory capacity, and 85% of the performance with 25% capacity. With a “memory-hungry” agent, AMD claims 90% and 88% performance for 50% and 25% capacity, respectively.

The slide you can see above has footnote tags. However, AMD has not shared the footnotes with us yet, so we don’t have a view into how these tests were run. Naturally, we assume AMD has, at minimum, represented the performance of MEXT in the best light possible. We can’t do a full analysis without knowing how the tests were run, however.

What is interesting is AMD’s cautious approach to rolling out MEXT. It’s an EPYC-exclusive feature right now, though AMD left the door open for support on future products (consumer devices, such as Strix Halo) far down the road. It will be sold as a license, bundled with the RAM View software, but we don’t have a timeline on when that will happen. And, despite a partnership with HPE to push out “MEXT Ready” servers, we still don’t know when MEXT itself will be ready for deployment beyond AMD’s walls.

Given that conservative approach, there are likely pitfalls to MEXT that we’re not seeing yet, and it’s hard to imagine it will be broadly applicable to every server, at least at the 50% and 25% DRAM capacity levels that AMD showed off with its benchmarks.

However, even being able to trim 25% of a server’s DRAM capacity represents a massive cost savings in the current supply-constrained environment. If some workloads can push that to 50% capacity, that’s even better. Of course, we’ll need to see how MEXT holds up once it’s available broadly, but if AMD’s claims hold water, it could become a defining technology in data centers that can’t seem to get enough memory.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

#10495. Your burnout may be a boundaries issue

Below, Nabeela Elsayed shares five key insights from her new book, Breaking Burnout: How High Achievers Break the Success Myths Driving Exhaustion, Overwork, and Burnout.

Nabeela is a recovering workaholic and former C-suite executive. She began her career as a barista making $6.50 an hour and spent the next 20-plus years climbing the corporate ladder until she ran operations and people at companies including Walmart Canada and IKEA.

What’s the Big Idea?

Burnout isn’t a stamina problem. It isn’t a boundaries problem. It’s what happens when the definition of success you were handed was never survivable in the first place. Getting off the burnout loop isn’t a dramatic leap. It’s a series of small choices toward a life that no longer costs you yourself.

Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Nabeela herself—in the Next Big Idea App, or buy the book.

1. Fix your relationship with work, not just your job.

When I lived in Sweden, I learned about lördagsgodis—Saturday candy. Kids and grown-ups skip sweets all week and enjoy them on Saturdays. This is a country with a pastry shop on every corner, yet an entire society says “not today” six out of seven days. That’s not willpower. Back in the 1940s and 1950s, dental researchers discovered that how often you eat sugar does more damage than how much. Health authorities said: if you’re going to have it, have it once a week. That became a ritual in families.

Sugar is not a villain, and neither is work itself. We need to work, but like food, it can nourish or poison you depending on how often and how intensely you consume it. Most of us assume the problem is the job—the toxic boss or impossible workload—and sometimes it is, but usually it is a toxic relationship with work itself.

You can be in a great company with a great boss, or even be the boss, and have an unhealthy relationship with work. Chris Raney built the world’s largest HR podcast platform. He owns the company. No one’s forcing him to do anything. And one morning he got up, did his workout, took a shower, and tried to head to work, but he couldn’t move. He was having a major anxiety attack, frozen at the threshold of his front door. When I talked to him about it, he said, “It’s self-inflicted. It’s all self-inflicted.”

Changing jobs rarely fixes burnout because you bring your relationship with work with you. So before you update your resume, ask yourself: how healthy is your relationship with work?

2. Ask whether rest restores you.

The sports world has figured out something the rest of us haven’t. Athletes don’t wait for an injury to find out that they’ve been overloaded. Lauren Bushman, director of sports science for Canada Basketball, and her team work backward from the moments that matter—the playoffs or Olympics—and build capacity slowly over years. Recovery isn’t a reward. It’s part of the training plan. As Lauren told me, “You never mess with a basketball player’s pre-game nap.” And her measure of success is beautifully simple: Are her players healthy and ready when it counts?

“Recovery isn’t a reward. It’s part of the training plan.”

Now, think about how most of us work. We run an endless marathon at sprint speed. Nobody’s tracking our load, and we’re usually the last to notice something’s off. But a simple question can improve self-awareness; ask yourself: Does rest restore you? Exhaustion is running out of gas. You can refill the tank with sleep or a weekend off or a real vacation, and your energy comes back. But burnout is the engine breaking down completely. You rest, and nothing changes. The cynicism is still there, the detachment is still there, and the joy doesn’t come back.

Horacio Barbeito, my former CEO at Walmart Canada, spent more than 30 years learning this the hard way. At one point, just hours before a flight, he cancelled a major conference trip rather than pushing through. He explained it perfectly: “I need to slow things down to go fast.” If rest restores you, then you’re tired, and that’s normal. If it doesn’t, that’s your signal to stop, act, and talk to a medical professional.

3. Trace your wiring.

Chester Elton is known worldwide as the Apostle of Appreciation. So when he told me that for the first part of his career he was “an absolute jerk,” I almost fell out of my chair.

Chester had what he calls a magical childhood—a big, loving family filled with faith and service. But he was the youngest of five boys, and if you didn’t eat fast, you didn’t eat. You worked hard, you competed, and you won. That followed him to school and into his career, and it paid off. Bigger house, great vacations, and the corner office. What he couldn’t see was who he was becoming. His wife Heidi would catch him yelling in the shower, replaying work conversations. Then one evening on a walk around the neighborhood, she said, “I don’t care what we do, but we are not doing this anymore. I want my husband back. This is not who you are.”

Even a happy childhood can teach you that effort is how good people prove they’re good, and that worth is something you earn. For a lot of us, the wiring goes back generations. Marj Rehman, founder of Envoi, comes from four generations of immigrants: India to Pakistan to Dubai to Canada. He told me there has always been an urgency in life, a feeling that there is no rest. As a child of immigrants myself, I know that feeling in my bones.

This is where the burnout loop starts. The wiring is set in childhood. Then a culture that celebrates overwork rewards it. Over time, a sacrifice starts to feel like obligation—until something forces you to stop. Ask yourself: who taught me what success looks like? And did anyone ever tell me when to stop?

4. Refuse to be a stump.

Years ago, I was driving home on a 10-lane highway in Houston, Texas, after a brutal day at work, and suddenly I couldn’t breathe. My chest was tight. I was dizzy. My whole body was shutting down. I pulled over and called 911 because I thought I was having a heart attack. The hospital discharged me, and the next morning I went back to work like nothing had happened. This is what I call the sacrifice myth in action. It’s the belief that if you want to be successful, it’s supposed to hurt.

“Over time, a sacrifice starts to feel like obligation—until something forces you to stop.”

You may have grown up with The Giving Tree. It’s a book about a boy and a tree, and the tree loves the boy. As the boy grows up, he takes her apples to sell, her branches to build a house, and her trunk to build a boat. At the end, there’s nothing left of her but a stump—and we’re told she’s happy. As a child, I thought it was a beautiful story of love. Now, as an adult, it makes me want to scream. It teaches us that love and loyalty are proven by disappearing. My teenager and I have a saying. When she sees me self-sacrifice, she puts her arm on my shoulder and she says, “Mom, don’t be a stump.”

We do this with work all the time. We give pain and sacrifice a purpose, and that’s supposed to make it better. We treat the suffering itself as proof that we’re serious, committed, and worthy. But work is an exchange. You give it your skill, your time, and your commitment. In return, you get a livelihood, growth, recognition, agency, and impact. When the price is your health, relationships, or humanity, it’s no longer an exchange. That is self-abandonment. That’s becoming a stump.

The opposite of martyrdom isn’t quiet quitting or bed rotting. It’s stewardship—taking care of your energy, knowing your limits, and building a life you can actually sustain.

5. Be more than your title.

Stacy Brown-Philpot spent nearly two decades climbing from Google to CEO of TaskRabbit, where she led the company through its acquisition by IKEA. When she stepped down, it was the first time in almost twenty years she didn’t have a title. She found herself asking, “If I’m not a CEO, then who am I?”

The offers kept coming—a public company, a private company, each one exactly what she was “supposed” to do next. People told her, “We don’t have enough Black women CEOs. You need to get back in there.”

That’s the identity myth: the idea that what I do is who I am. What makes it so insidious is that we’re rewarded for it. If you start disappearing into a romantic relationship, someone who loves you will pull you aside; if you disappear into your work, you’ll get applauded.

“What makes it so insidious is that we’re rewarded for it.”

Every job has an end, whether that means a layoff or retirement. If your whole self lives in one role, losing that role feels like losing yourself. Think of it like a house: work isn’t the foundation. It’s an important room that, during some seasons, you’ll spend a lot of time in. But you can’t board up every other room for 20 years.

I once opened a session for senior leaders with a simple question: “Tell me who you are without telling me what you do.” Long pauses. Nervous laughter. Most of them had never reflected on that question. So try it. You might be someone’s steady presence, the friend who remembers birthdays, the neighbor who shovels the snow, or the person in your family who makes a mean stack of pancakes. Those aren’t small things. Those are the joys that life is built on.

Stop pretending you’re fine. Stop pretending your life can wait until the next milestone.

#10494. A Practical Introduction to the Twitch Helix API

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Behind almost every Twitch tool you have ever seen, the stat trackers, the moderation bots, the stream overlays, the alert systems, sits one interface: the Twitch Helix API. Twitch is unusually generous with public data, and Helix is the door to it. If you have ever wondered how third-party sites know who is live, what a channel's viewership looks like, or details a Twitch profile page does not even display, this is the machinery.

This article is a practical overview of Helix for developers who have not used it yet: what it offers, how its authentication works, what people build with it, and where the sharp edges are.

Helix is Twitch's current REST API, served from api.twitch.tv/helix. It replaced the old "Kraken" API, which was fully retired in 2022, so any tutorial still showing Kraken endpoints is a sign to keep scrolling. Helix covers users, streams, channels, games and categories, clips, chat, moderation actions, subscriptions, and events, with JSON in and JSON out.

Two things distinguish it from many platform APIs. First, a large share of it works without any user's permission, because the data is public by Twitch's own definition. Second, it is paired with EventSub, a push system that notifies your application when things happen (a stream goes live, a user follows, a message arrives) instead of forcing you to poll. Most serious Twitch tools use both: Helix for lookups, EventSub for live events.

Authentication is where most newcomers stall, mainly because Twitch offers several OAuth flows and tutorials rarely say which one you actually need. The short version:

Every request needs a Client ID, which you get by registering an application in the Twitch developer console (two-factor authentication on your account is required first). Requests carry the Client ID and a bearer token together; forgetting the Client ID header is the classic mystery 401.

App access tokens come from the client credentials flow, a single server-to-server request with your ID and secret. They have no user attached and that is fine, because public reads, user profiles, live streams, top games, clips, need no user context. For most read-only tools, this is the only flow you ever touch.

Tokens expire, so real applications cache them with their reported lifetime and refresh on a 401 rather than assuming a token lives forever.

A tour of the endpoints that power most tools:

Users. Give the users endpoint a username and it returns the account's public record: display name, profile image, description, Affiliate or Partner status, and the account's exact creation timestamp. That last field is interesting because Twitch does not display it anywhere on a profile, yet it is one of the platform's most useful trust signals, moderators use account age to spot throwaway accounts, and streamers use it to filter giveaway entries. The creation date alone powers a small subcategory of tools: free account age checkers, such as Twitch account age checker, are essentially this one endpoint with a clean page around it, taking any public username and returning the creation date, age, avatar, and broadcaster status. It is a good illustration of how far a single well-chosen Helix field can go.

Streams. The stream's endpoint reports who is live right now, with titles, categories, thumbnail URLs, and viewer counts. This is the backbone of every "is my favorite streamer live" notifier and every directory-style site, and polling it over time is how stat trackers chart viewership history.

Games and categories. Top games, category search, and metadata. Combined with streams data, this is how analytics sites rank categories and how tools answer "how crowded is this category right now."

Clips and videos. Clip metadata, view counts, and creation tools. Highlight compilers and clip-sharing bots live here.

Helix enforces a points-based rate limit per Client ID, and every response tells you where you stand through Ratelimit-Limit, Ratelimit-Remaining, and Ratelimit-Reset headers. Well-behaved tools read those headers and back off before hitting zero; badly behaved ones retry 429s in a loop and wonder why things get worse. For lookup-style tools the practical fix is caching, data like account creation dates never changes, so there is no reason to ask twice.

A few more edges worth knowing before they bite:

Usernames change, IDs do not. Store user IDs, not logins, or your saved data will eventually point at the wrong person.

Missing users are not errors. Looking up a nonexistent username returns a successful response with an empty data array, so handle the empty case explicitly.

Batching exists. The users endpoint takes up to 100 logins in one call, which matters the moment your tool checks lists instead of individuals.

Secrets stay server-side. The client secret identifies your application; calling the token endpoint from browser code hands your app's identity to anyone who opens devtools. Public-facing tools put a small server between the browser and Twitch.

The reason Twitch's third-party ecosystem is so large is that the barrier is so low: one public API, generous free access, and a platform where small questions genuinely matter to people. That is why the space is full of narrow tools that each answer one thing well, when was this account created, is this channel live, how fast is this category growing, which clips popped this week. Most of them are a weekend of work on top of one or two endpoints, and some of them grow into real products.

If you want to start, the path is short: register an application at the developer console, request an app access token, and call the users or streams endpoint for something you actually care about. The official documentation at dev.twitch.tv is current and well maintained, which is not something every platform can claim. Pick one piece of data Twitch collects but does not display, put a clean interface on it, and you are following the same recipe as most of the Twitch tools you already use.

#10492. Samsung Galaxy S27 series camera specs leak, and they’re disappointing

New leaks reveal the camera specs for Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series which includes three lenses across the lineup, but not the upgrades you want, nor what Ultra owners might expect.

SammyGuru reports that Samsung is “evaluating” camera setups for the Galaxy S27, S27+, S27 Pro, and S27 Ultra, and it looks like a mixed bag across the board.

The base Galaxy S27 and S27+ are looking very familiar, with identical main camera sensors to last year, and the same ultrawide sensor that’s been in use since the Galaxy S23 series. The telephoto and selfie sensors are looking at new hardware, but without any major spec upgrades.

Galaxy S27 Pro and Ultra, meanwhile, have a new 200MP main camera on deck, a 50MP ultrawide shooter, and a mere 12MP telephoto. The Ultra might get 5x compared to the Pro’s 3x optical zoom, but with a secondary telephoto lens going missing, existing users of the lineup are sure to be disappointed.

Notably, SammyGuru’s article mentions the Pro as using “the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s 3x sensor,” but shows the 12MP Samsung S5K3LD in that place instead. We’re assuming that’s a typo seeing as the post mentions the Pro as using the Samsung S5KJN3 or the Sony IMX855 earlier on, but regardless, the Pro only gets 3x optical zoom to the Ultra’s 5x.

Some of these specs have been mentioned by other sources such as GalaxyClub and leaker Ice Universe, but this is the most complete picture of the S27’s camera plans we’ve seen to date.

Personally, I’m very “whelmed” on this one. As RAMageddon rages on and Samsung hunts for new ways to balance specs vs price, cameras are a place that’s obviously going to be cut, but competitors are already running laps around Samsung on the hardware front. Cutting lenses and skimping out on upgrades (again) doesn’t help matters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Linux Kernel is probably one of the best ecosystems to observe regarding the impact of AI in programming. The critical importance of its code and its maintainers' quality standards mean that patches, including but not only AI slop, go through rigorous review and are often discarded. Still, the amount of AI-produced code is often far higher than what the human reviewers can deal with. Lorenzo Stoakes, a lead Linux reviewer for memory management, has elected to step down from some of his former duties for exactly that reason.

Stoakes announced his decision today in a thread on the Linux kernel mailing list (LKML). He'll be leaving the core, reclaim, Rust, THP (Huge Pages), and miscellaneous sections of the kernel memory management section, while staying on for his remaining duties, including KVM. The partial departure appears amicable, and the developer doesn't appear to be angry or bitter. He says that his decision was due to the mounting pressure on his inbox, that he'll wrap up the patch series he's currently working on, and he'll occasionally pitch in regardless.

However, the underlying cause is also clear: "Of course the AI wave has been horrible, and is getting significantly worse. At first it was once in a while that I'd see slop. Then it was at least once a week. Then every few days. Nowadays it's pretty much half of what I see, if not more."

This is a sentiment echoed by many programmers in the open-source community, and the latest in a running series of AI-provoked project departures, submission rules adjustments, and strategic shifts. AI-assisted programming has arguably been both a boon and a curse for open-source software. The project's open nature means that anyone can find a bug and report it or fix it, or add functionality — all of which are good things.

However, that also means that literally anyone can contribute, and in a world ridden with low-effort AI slop and untold amounts of AI agents, that's... suboptimal. Open-source projects are arguably the hardest-hit because they very rarely have the adequate manpower or funds to keep the code up to date, much less deal with the output of a million robotic monkeys on a million digital typewriters.

Linus Torvalds, creator and headmaster of Linux, has taken a pro-AI stance, supported not only by the speed of additional contributions, but also the fact that bots often don't make mistakes that even seasoned developers do. This topic has been the subject of a lot of LKML discussion, and the current stance is that AI-assisted code commits don't need to be marked as such.

The problem, then, has arguably become one of filtering: it's easy enough to be accepting of AI contributions when your day isn't spent waddling through mud to find the one gold nugget, which is what Stoakes was seemingly weary of.

Back in July, he'd already brought up concerns about the "recent wave of slop in [memory management]," adding that "the amount of time wasted on AI slop is already too much and we're only at the start of this." Even as recently as a month ago, he said that "what kills the project is having 1,000 slop submissions that 2 or 3 people have to do something with."

#10490. Friday the 13th is here. Its impact on your work day may not be so scary

Business can be risky, so it’s natural that superstitions can sometimes creep in when money and careers are at stake.

This workweek ends on Friday the 13th, so in the Western world, the stage is set for fear to influence commerce.

Let’s take a look at the so-called bad luck day’s origins and how it impacts the business world.

What is a fear of Friday the 13th called?

A fear of Friday the 13th is called “paraskevidekatriaphobia,” a term created by psychotherapist Donald Dossey. It combines the Greek words for Friday, 13, and fear.

How many Friday the 13ths are there in a year?

Around every 212.35 days, a Friday the 13th occurs. This figure is based on a complete 400-year Gregorian calendar cycle.

Another way to look at it: there is at least one Friday the 13th a year, but there can be up to three. This year, 2026, Friday the 13th will be in triplicate.

When did Friday the 13th become unlucky?

The truth is, no one really knows how exactly Friday the 13th became synonymous with misfortune.

There are historical and religious references that might shed some light. One of the theories is that the number 12 is considered perfect and complete, so by comparison, 13 is less than.

A popular retelling of Norse mythology states that 12 gods were having a banquet in Valhalla until Loki showed up uninvited, bringing their numbers to 13. The unwelcome guest was able to trick the blind god Höd into killing his brother Balder.

The number 13 and the day Friday also show up in Christianity. According to Christian teachings, there were 13 people present at the Last Supper, which occurred on a Thursday.

The following day, Jesus was crucified. Many also believe Eve gave Adam the forbidden fruit from the tree of knowledge and Cain killed Abel on a Friday.

Where does Friday the 13th show up in pop culture?

History does have examples of traumatic events happening on Friday the 13th. One of these occurred in 1307 when King Philip IV of France detained numerous members of the Knights Templar. Some of these men were eventually executed.

Friday the 13th also shows up in literature. In 1834, an article in Revue de Paris by Marquis de Salvo, entitled “Le Chateau de Carini,” told the story of a filicide committed by a Sicilian count on Friday the 13th.

In 1907, American author Thomas William Lawson published the novel Friday, the Thirteenth, about a stockbroker who crashes the market on the title date.

Perhaps the best modern example of Friday the 13th mania is Sean S. Cunningham’s slasher film franchise, which began in 1980. Jason Voorhees’s hockey goalie mask has become iconic.

Crystal Lake, a prequel series produced by A24, is the latest from the franchise and currently streaming on Peacock.

How does superstition impact business?

In 2006, the same Dr. Dossey, who named the fear of Friday the 13th, also claimed Americans lost $800 to $900 million due to lost productivity driven by fear of the day. However, his nontransparent methodology to get to those figures has drawn criticism. The Wall Street Journal is just one of the publications that questioned its validity.

Although it’s hard to quantify an exact figure, the impact of the fear of Friday the 13th can be found.

In Manhattan and Brooklyn, less than 5% of mid-rise and high-rise residential condo buildings have a floor labeled 13, WSJ reports.

According to Realting.com, 13th-floor apartments are purchased 18% less often on average than their counterparts located on other floors. Apartment sales are also down on the day itself, 19% on any given 13th.

Ironically, a 2007 USA Today/Gallup poll found that only 13% of Americans would be bothered if required to stay on the 13th floor of a hotel. A spooky statistic indeed.

#10487. Samsung’s paid Galaxy AI plan has a giant Gemini problem

Good morning. Today I’m trying desperately not to buy Sony’s new nostalgia-bait headphones, reeling from how emotionally invested I was in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (yes, I know I’m late), trying to figure out what a “private, agentic notebook” is, and slowly coming around to the idea of the New York Times owning Letterboxd.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

The relationship between Samsung and Google has, over the years, waxed and waned depending on their respective interdependence. Samsung is Android’s physical emissary, powering a plurality of all its handsets globally. But Google, and in particular its services, is the glue that holds Samsung’s smartphone experience together.

The back and forth is over a decade old; back in early 2014, Samsung shipped a refreshed magazine-style skin with its Galaxy tablets that eschewed many of the design tenets Google had been pushing its partners to adhere to. Not only was Samsung willfully defying its most important partner, but it made a point of barely mentioning Android during its press conferences.

Around the same time, it transitioned its smartwatches from Android Wear to Tizen and began shipping duplicative apps on its devices (many of which persist to this day). The goal was to distance itself from Google as much as possible.

While we don’t know exactly what happened behind closed doors, we saw the outcome quite clearly: Magazine UX lasted one product cycle, and the two companies signed a 10-year cross-license patent deal, which may have helped Samsung prevent any future lawsuits with Apple. Google then sold Motorola to Lenovo, clearing the way for Samsung to continue building its burgeoning hardware business on the back of Google’s mobile ecosystem.

Since then, the two companies have grown even closer. In 2021, they co-announced a new Wear OS along with an overarching wearables partnership that has since grown to include Android XR as well. And Google is still the default search engine for Samsung devices, despite reported inroads made by Microsoft in 2023 to convince the Korean giant to switch to a ChatGPT-powered version of Bing Search. (Samsung’s ongoing relationship with Microsoft, which bundles its Office suite on most Galaxy devices, could be seen as a point of leverage for negotiations with Google, too.)

This brings us to today, and to AI. Samsung was among the first companies to adopt Google’s full suite of Gemini Intelligence products, and its phones often get new AI features before anyone else. But like a decade ago, when Samsung shipped Bixby to kind-of-sort-of compete with Google Assistant, it still wants to offer its own services alongside Google’s.

So a rumor that Samsung may launch a paid Galaxy AI Premium subscription next year for $5/month piqued my interest for the same reason Magazine UX did 12 years ago. Galaxy AI features today are a blend of first-party and third-party capabilities, but none of them are especially useful, particularly when compared to Google’s own Android equivalents powered by Gemini Intelligence. Now Bar and Now Brief, two heavily promoted features in Samsung’s marketing, are wildly disappointing.

At I/O this past May, Google announced Spark, an agent that goes out and performs actions on your behalf. And while it’s since been somewhat eclipsed by more capable mobile options like Meta’s Muse, it’s obvious that Google is working on a follow-up that will perform functions both on the phone and inside apps.

That’s exactly what Samsung is rumored to be working on with Bixby Action, a spiritual successor to its namesake that, when it debuted, prioritized on-device tasks like turning on Wi-Fi over web-based actions Google Assistant did better.

According to leaks from SamMobile, Galaxy AI Premium will offer agentic upgrades for phone users to “create commands triggers and system routines for daily tasks” or “automate routine daily tasks using Galaxy AI.” Gen Video will reportedly “convert static photos into dynamic video clips,” while a new Daily Briefing likely does what it says on the tin.

Will Samsung users see enough value in this hodgepodge of features paywalled only because they use a surfeit of compute? And what models will power them on the backend?

Right now, Google is in the enviable position of being able to offer its AI at three distinct layers: the model itself, which is invisible to the user; the OS level, which can promulgate Gemini across every Android phone that runs Google services; and the hardware level, where Pixel lets it specialize and optimize.

Samsung, not particularly known for its software prowess, will likely need to step gingerly around Google’s AI shadow while also justifying the cost to shore up its much-needed services revenue. Based on this leaked roadmap, though, I’m not confident it will work out.

Instead, Samsung may want to acquire one of the many up-and-coming AI agent startups whose valuations are rising more quickly than their user bases. While Muse and OpenAI’s Dots have taken up most of the recent conversation, I’ve been using Hark, Town, and Instinct pretty regularly for a month or so and could see them being brought in-house by Samsung and offered either as standalone products or customized for Galaxy devices. As Google is doing with its own AI plans, Samsung could provide Galaxy users a year of free service, after which they would be expected to pay.

Samsung doesn’t have a great history of building software, but many of its acquisitions, from SmartThings to Viv Labs (which became “next-gen” Bixby) to LoopPay (which became Samsung Pay) to Whisk (which became Samsung Food), have proven successful. Given the current urgent state of mobile AI, I’d forgo the hodgepodge and bring in some outside expertise.

Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy is the only thing tech media can talk about right now, likely because it has implications far beyond just Nvidia’s stock price. The Nvidia CEO, who is one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech executives, is believed to have been targeted by Chinese intelligence to potentially influence American trade policy around AI.

Alex Kantrowitz’s Big Technology piece is a useful starting point for why this matters at a global scale:

Beyond the affair, the real issue is that Huang’s love interest, ex-Megaspeed International executive Alice Huang, is someone the United States government believes passed information to the Chinese government while building data centers with Nvidia’s help in Asia. There’s simply no getting away from this detail. This isn’t just an affair, it’s a corporate and national security issue.

Whether Huang can survive the impending investigation by Nvidia’s board remains to be seen, but the CEO has been a stalwart in the tech space for 33 years, and there is no clear successor to his position should he be forced to resign.

Damien reviewed DroidDeck, which I wrote about last week as part of a broader look at Android’s gaming renaissance.

Over the last few days, things have become even more preposterous: the Ocarina of Time remake, which was released on Thursday, has already been recompiled to run natively on Android (though it runs better on PC), largely with the help of frontier AI models.

All of these AI-powered shenanigans come after Anthropic said it would stop making it possible to recreate copies of games, claiming that “recreating someone else’s specific game using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.” Good thing there are no other models capable of doing the same thing.

I think when you zoom out and look at production, AI really has the potential to be the biggest creative unlock in modern history. The last time we saw anything close to this was really the, you know, advent of CGI and digital composites in the early ’90s. That technology gave birth to amazing stories like Jurassic Park and Terminator 2, and it’s hard to imagine that AI is not going to have a more significant impact than that. And I personally believe that’s going to be an incredible unlock on creativity.

—David Ellison, Skydance CEO, when asked about how AI could impact the movie-making process

Thanks for reading, and have a great day. I’ll talk to you on Thursday.

#10485. How to survive the loss of an irreplaceable leader

The challenge of replacing Jensen Huang, the visionary co-founder and CEO of Nvidia, who resigned yesterday morning amid reports of extramarital affairs, may be daunting—but it is far from unprecedented.

While research shows that companies moving on from a founding CEO face a higher risk of failure or downturn than other CEO transitions, major corporations from Apple to Amazon have successfully managed the loss of a larger-than-life presence at the top of the corporate ladder.

Management experts who have studied such transitions say there are a few key lessons.

Don’t look for a carbon copy of the founder

When Tim Cook replaced legendary Apple founder Steve Jobs in 2011, speculation suggested he might try to replicate Jobs’ style, right down to the signature turtleneck and jeans. However, experts warned against directly replicating Jobs’ leadership and management style.

 “A copy of anyone is going to come off looking bad,” Wharton management professor Peter Cappelli said. “It will never be as good as the original, and people will spend their time focusing on the differences.”

Cook succeeded by building on Apple’s strengths and emphasizing his expertise as an operations specialist, scaling the sophisticated global supply chain he helped build as chief operating officer to increase annual revenue nearly fourfold.

Instead of positioning himself as a visionary like his legendary predecessor, Cook maintained an understated management style and let the company’s massive financial success speak for itself. Cook says he urged his own successor, John Ternus, to take his own individual approach.

“Don’t mimic me, just like I didn’t mimic Steve,” Cook recalled telling Ternus in a recent interview with The Independent. “We all have different strengths.”

Give the successor real authority—and make sure the founder lets go

While research shows transitions are more successful when founders feel involved in the planning process, once they step down, it is important they keep their distance.

“The presence of two prominent leaders can confuse the organization and hinder the success of the successor CEO,” executive search firm Spencer Stuart wrote in 2024. “There can only be one CEO.”

The firm recommends having explicit conversations among the founder, successor, and the board to clearly distinguish the founder’s responsibilities from those of the new chief executive.

Spencer Stuart also examined 200 U.S. companies with executive chairmen (leaders, often former or founding executives, who preside over the board of directors while also remaining involved in daily business operations and management) and found that 54% underperformed their peers during the executive chair’s tenure—by an average of 14%.

Give the corporate culture room to breathe

Often, successful founders dictate not only their company’s strategy but also its internal culture. Workplace norms, management practices, and the company’s identity become a reflection of their personal style and values. While employees can become deeply attached to those traditions, that doesn’t mean they will work for the founder’s successor.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has spoken frequently about how he adjusted the company’s culture after taking over from Bill Gates’ successor, Steve Ballmer, in 2014.

Sensing that the company needed to rethink its hard-charging internal culture, Nadella sought to reduce internal division and promote collaboration: in his words, move from a “know-it-all” mindset to a “learn-it-all” one. One of his policies was to ensure individual performance reviews reflected how employees contributed to others’ success.

“Achieving our mission requires us to evolve our culture,” Nadella says. “It all starts with a growth mindset—a passion to learn and bring our best every day to make a bigger difference in the world.”

The changes accompanied a broader strategic transformation that helped Microsoft become a leader in cloud computing and AI. Annual revenue has more than tripled, from $87 billion in 2014 to $282 billion in 2025.

Start by planning ahead

Unfortunately for Nvidia, it appears the company has not engaged in what many experts consider one of the most important aspects of a smooth transition: planning ahead. The best chief executives work with their directors on succession planning throughout their tenure to ensure the company is protected in an emergency.

According to McKinsey, former Intuit CEO Brad Smith gave the board a quarterly verbal update on his succession plan and held an official succession planning session once a year. During the session, company leaders would consider potential candidates and adjust their criteria for the next CEO to adapt to the market.

Experts also say the best transitions often have a firm timeline.  

“Without a clear timetable, grooming internal successors and following an orderly succession process become challenging,” former Medtronic CEO and Harvard Business School professor Bill George has said.  

For Nvidia, the preparation may have to happen in reverse. Huang spent more than three decades building a company around his technical vision, unconventional management style, and personal authority. His successor will now have to determine which parts of that legacy are essential to Nvidia’s success—and which can be jettisoned.

In fact, this transition might be the final test of Huang’s leadership. In the words of management expert Jim Collins: “If your company cannot be great without you, it is not yet a great company.”

Intel and AMD NPU support is planned, but founder says neither will be used for language models.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A team led by Cyanogen co-founder Kirt McMaster has unveiled Kora, a new Linux desktop OS with integrated AI models and agents that can split workloads across CPU, GPU, and NPU resources, as well as other machines on the same local network. We reached out to the firm for more info.

Kora, the first product from Kora Systems Inc., previously Playtron, carries the tagline “The Operating System for Intelligence” and has its own Cortex “hybrid inference engine” technology, which is not open source and is optimized for local models. The OS, built “from the kernel to the shell,” runs local models by default and cloud models when needed, and is expected to arrive on PCs in 2027.

The desktop follows the AI-focused motif with “neural workspaces” and a “neural file system,” which refer to sandboxed workspaces and files indexed by semantic meaning. Kora has three operating modes: “Work," "Create," and "Play." That last base is covered by GameFrame, which descends from Playtron’s GameOS. Humain OS, which Kora is developing with Saudi AI company Humain, is the enterprise variant of this OS.

Currently, the only NPU named in the release material is the Hexagon NPU found in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, which Qualcomm pegs at 80 TOPS. On the X2 Elite, Cortex can schedule AI workloads across the CPU, GPU, and NPU, as well as other systems on the local network, which could be a novel capability if it works beyond the Qualcomm hardware.

McMaster told Tom’s Hardware that the Snapdragon X2 Elite NPU runs Google's Gemma 4 26B model at 25 tokens per second for decode. Intel and AMD NPU support is in the works, but according to the developer, neither NPU will be used for LLMs, as GPUs are “just better for LLM workloads on x64.”

Each NPU vendor has its own software stack, or runtime, and prefers that models are compiled in its own format: Qualcomm with QAIRT/QNN, Intel with OpenVINO, and AMD with Ryzen AI software. The press kit doesn't identify support for any Intel or AMD chip, NPU runtime, model format, quantization, or speed figures for those platforms.

Our earlier Windows testing showed the same kind of divide: Snapdragon reached its NPU through the QNN provider under ONNX Runtime, while Intel’s work ran through IPEX, its extension for PyTorch, on the GPU because it was faster than the NPU.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

When asked about cross-vendor support, McMaster reiterated that “only Hexagon on Snapdragon X2 Elite is supported today.” Intel NPU support is planned, with “conversations underway,” though McMaster later clarified that neither Intel’s nor AMD’s NPU will be used for LLMs. On AMD’s Ryzen AI chips, Kora will likely use the NPU for embedding and speech-recognition models through ONNX.As for what drives the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU, McMaster said Kora uses the “llama.cpp Hexagon backend” and “the upstream FastRPC driver.” That suggests the operating system reaches the NPU through the open-source llama.cpp project, not Qualcomm’s own QAIRT/QNN runtime, by way of the FastRPC driver in the mainline kernel.

Language models; KORA cites Gemma 4 26B at 25 tokens per second

Likely embedding and speech-recognition models; not language models

When asked about model formats, McMaster said, “we predominantly support GGUF,” llama.cpp’s model file format, and that Lemma, the inference engine inside Cortex, “can split model layers across processors as needed.” Lemma is built on llama.cpp, whisper.cpp, stable-diffusion.cpp, and ONNX. McMaster says that which runtime is used depends on the model's requirements, and more runtimes will be added down the line.

For today, llama.cpp has a Hexagon backend for Snapdragon and an OpenVINO backend for Intel CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, although the latter is still marked “In Progress,” and no AMD NPU backend, which would explain why AMD goes through ONNX. AMD NPUs can run LLMs on Linux through the separate Lemonade 10.0 stack with FastFlowLM, as reported by Phoronix in March, though that isn’t the route Kora has chosen.

Beyond NPU stacks, those hoping to run Kora will need to be mindful of their system's available memory. The Gemma 4 26B model Kora uses, which Google lists as Gemma 4 26B A4B, needs about 14.4GB of memory to load its weights at 4-bit (Q4_0) quantization, by Google’s estimate, before any context window, while third-party listings put the download for the Q4_K_M file Kora uses at about 16–17GB. The model only activates about 4 billion of its 26 billion parameters per token but still needs to be fully loaded into memory.

McMaster said that with the model, the X2 Elite reaches “25 TPS decode throughput and 550 TPS prefill throughput,” or tokens per second, running “entirely on the Hexagon NPU with 32K context.” A dense model, rather than a mixture-of-experts, would be far slower. Not given are the RAM configuration or the specific X2 Elite chip.

On memory, McMaster said that “we recommend 64GB because it gives you access to better models,” but that is not a firm requirement. The company projects that “about 70 percent of the model calls it manages will run locally in 2027.”

Kora says its enterprise-focused Humain OS is due first and will be “commercially available in 2027,” on OEM PCs using the Snapdragon X2 Elite. Kora will follow "later in 2027.”

McMaster says that “Kora will be posted on our site and downloadable for anyone to install.” Included will be a list of recommended configurations, “but it should be installable on most modern PCs.” Exact pricing and the overall business model will be shared closer to the date of availability.Edit: 11/11/2026 9:06am PT: Added further follow-up details provided by the maker.

#10481. Forget ‘sponsored’ tags in AI answers. Agent loyalty is what matters

No one loves ads, but generally people will tolerate them if it means getting something free or at a lower price. What people won’t forgive? Being lied to.

A study looking at how consumers see native ads on news sites—which look similar to editorial content, just with labels—found that fewer than 10% of consumers could identify them as advertising. And when people find out after the fact, they don’t take it well. In a Contently survey, two-thirds of readers said they felt deceived when they realized an article or video was sponsored by a brand.

That’s why there’s a whole set of regulations and standards around advertising disclosures that are meant to protect consumers. Now that AI is slowly becoming a central part of our media ecosystem, it’s unclear to what extent those disclosures should carry over into AI answers. After all, if the public is increasingly using AI to shop (47% of U.S. shoppers who use AI started their last product search with AI, according to an impact.com survey, and Meta says shopping is the most common use of its new personal AI agent, Muse), it feels intuitive that the user should see plainly the commercial interests of the sites that informed any answer.

Truth in labeling?

A reliable label in AI sounds like a good idea, but it gets complicated quickly. For starters, the label might cause confusion that the AI platform itself was paid rather than the original publisher. In the case of ChatGPT that would potentially conflict with its own ads, which are separate from the answer and labeled as sponsored. OpenAI’s answer to the disclosure question, so far, is the citation link: since launching ChatGPT search, it has included links to sources in answers so users can check them for themselves.

All of this gets at the fundamental question of judgment, and which parts of judging a source users have handed over to AI, consciously or unconsciously, simply by using it. When you ask AI to come up with, say, recommendations for air fryers, it’s more like hiring a researcher, not looking at a billboard. In fact, some people turn to AI precisely to get away from the billboards: 24% of the shoppers in the impact.com survey said they use AI to avoid sponsored results and ads. You trust it to hoover up all the information it can find about the question, weigh all the factors—including whether or not any sources are sponsored—and give you the best possible answer.

How important is a label at that point? It’d be silly to ask a researcher to stamp every brochure they look at, and pass those brochures over to you in a pile. If AI can solve some of humanity’s most intractable math problems, it can probably reliably weigh the commercial intent of a brand’s FAQ page. In fact, you could argue a label in the answer might cause the reader to overscrutinize an answer the AI has already deemed the most useful possible.

AI’s affiliate addiction

If we’re considering disclosures, we need to talk about affiliate content, and AI’s outsize reliance on it. As you might imagine, for any query about buying decisions, AI seeks out product recommendations. Those articles are often supported by affiliate revenue, meaning the site gets a fee when the reader takes action, typically a purchase. Legitimate sites that monetize via affiliate disclose that fact on any page with affiliate links; indeed, FTC guidelines require that they do so.

However, almost none of those disclosures survive the journey into an AI answer. AI summaries rely heavily on affiliate content: one study found that about a quarter of the pages cited by ChatGPT, Google’s AI Overviews, and Perplexity carried a commercial disclosure, and 86% of answers cited at least one such page. If those disclosures carried over, they’d be in almost every shopping answer. Beyond the UI nightmare that would result, would the label have any meaning at that point?

To be clear, no one’s arguing that disclosures don’t matter generally. Journalists take them very seriously, and they should. The SPJ code says to “distinguish news from advertising and shun hybrids that blur the lines.” Recommendation sites like Wirecutter or The Strategist make their business model clear, on every page, to everyone who cares to know.

The number of people who care to know, however, is likely rather low. When Pew tracked how people actually use Google, they clicked a link inside an AI summary on just 1% of visits. According to impact.com’s survey, Gen Z is split between those who never click through (11%) and those who always do (21%). That doesn’t contradict the anger over native ads: People hate finding out they were misled, but that’s different from wanting to audit every source up front. Again, auditing the sources is exactly the job they’re handing to the AI. While it wouldn’t solve all issues, you can picture a world where AI users have the option of seeing labels or not, perhaps via something like a “flag paid sources” toggle.

The kickback question

The label debate, however, misses the real concern. Anyone familiar with today’s models understands that AI can tell the difference between paid content and editorial (being able to tell isn’t the same as being impossible to game, but that’s another column). What is less clear are the commercial interests of the platform itself. In the researcher analogy, you might trust the judgment of the person you hired—that’s why you hired them. But you also want to be assured they’re not getting kickbacks from anyone they’re recommending. That worry isn’t hypothetical. In a University of Michigan study, people rarely noticed when a chatbot wove ads into its responses, and many actually preferred those answers. Even when the ads were labeled, about half the participants didn’t spot them.

This concern is at the heart of OpenAI’s promise that “ads do not influence the answers ChatGPT gives you,” which is directly from its ad principles. Ads only appear in ChatGPT’s free and Go tiers, and they always appear separate from the answer itself. Perplexity made similar promises when advertising was part of its business model, though it walked away from ads earlier this year, with one executive saying, “A user needs to believe this is the best possible answer.”

OpenAI’s promise is important because of the trust factor, which is evident when you look at conversion rates. Conversion from OpenAI ads is considerably lower than from the answers themselves. Early research from the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management found shoppers who clicked ChatGPT ads bought at a rate of 0.37%, versus 2.21% for those who arrived through ChatGPT’s regular answers. 

That makes sense—the answer gives what the model deems the “right” recommendation whereas an ad is just one of those options trying to sell you something. It also explains why OpenAI has every reason to keep that wall up. The moment answers look bought, they’ll convert like ads. Logically, this incentivizes brands to prioritize presence in AI answers over advertising. Not only are you more likely to drive business, you can also reach the people who pay for ChatGPT, who never see ads at all (and thus are more likely to pay for other things, like your product).

As I found out in my tests with Meta’s Muse, it will generally recommend what you can actually buy within Muse. When I asked it which robot vacuum was the best for me, it recommended a model that I could check out right there, but was not the top model on the review it cited. And Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said directly that Muse would monetize via transactions. On Meta’s October earnings call, he said the company will “build commerce tools so we get paid a fee based on the transactions that we help facilitate.” That suggests Muse will have every reason to consider what’s best for Meta when it steers you toward product decisions.

An agent you can trust

Concerns over agent influence have sparked calls for engineering “loyalty by design” in agentic systems, a phrase from Consumer Reports’ work on AI agents. The idea: agents should always put the needs and desires of the user first, and make transparent any other considerations, or even conflicts, they might have when finding information or carrying out actions. Sen. Mark Warner has floated draft legislation that would write a similar duty of loyalty into law for some AI agents.

There’s a strong case to be made that the market will correct for this: If any particular agent doesn’t act in the user’s interest in a material way, there’s certainly plenty of competition. That assumes switching is easy, though. An agent that knows your email, your calendar and what you bought last month is a lot harder to fire than a search engine.

Ultimately the fight over commercial labels is a good instinct, but it aims the question of trust at the wrong target. By using AI, I’m implicitly trusting the agent’s judgment to find the best information to answer my query. The better question is whether the agent is loyal, and how I can check. Labels protect readers from sketchy sources. What protects us from sketchy agents hasn’t been invented yet.

#10480. Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

LangSmith is closed-source and restricts self-hosting to enterprise licenses, teams that run their own LLMOps stack and want to keep traces on their own servers need an alternative. To find the best fit, we set a baseline by tracing a small TypeScript agent (equipped with two tools) in LangSmith Cloud. Then, we ran the exact same agent through Langfuse, Arize Phoenix, Opik, and AcruxCore using each platform's recommended TypeScript setup. All tests were run on November 5, 2026, and we pulled every trace back through each tool's API to verify the data.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree for the test prompt: a single agent span containing three LLM calls and two tool calls. The real differences between them come down to how much boilerplate code you have to write, how spans are typed, whether costs are tracked, and the overall server footprint.

Why Teams Look for a LangSmith Alternative

LangSmith remains the best choice if you already use LangChain and allow cloud hosting—it required just 25 lines of code in our test. The alternatives below are for teams that don't fit that profile.

To test these platforms, we built a simple customer support agent equipped with two tools:

Both tools use static fixture data to ensure every test run is identical. The agent runs a standard loop: it prompts the model, executes any requested tools, and stops once the model provides a final answer.

We tested the agent with three specific prompts to see how the tracing handled different levels of complexity:

For our comparison, we focused entirely on the third question because it generates a robust, multi-step trace.

Under the hood, the agent uses the standard openai package to call the qwen3.8-flash model. We originally picked this model based on its reliable tool-calling behavior during early probing thought it once skipped a tool call later.

We used LangSmith as our baseline. By tracing the agent there first, we created a checklist of every field it captured, and we judged all the alternatives against that exact list.

For setup, we followed the recommended TypeScript approach from each tool's documentation. Phoenix didn't have specific instructions for using its register() helper with OpenAI in TypeScript, so we adapted the pattern from their Anthropic guide.

Here is the agent with no tracing. Each tool section adds one tracing file that imports these files and changes nothing in them.

LangSmith traces the plain openai package with two helpers. wrapOpenAI records each model call, and traceable records your own functions. Without traceable on the run and the tools, wrapOpenAI alone gave three separate root runs and no tool runs.

This file adds 25 lines and removes 3, and installs one package.

LangSmith showed one root run with five children in call order: LLM, get_order_status, LLM, get_refund_policy, LLM. Every field it recorded became a row of the checklist table under "Results". Cost appeared only after a custom price entry. In our error run the failing tool was marked as an error, but the root stayed success: traceable turned the throw into a rejected promise that our agent did not await, so the agent carried on and answered.

Langfuse self-hosts as six containers, including ClickHouse, a column store built for large scans. In our measurement the stack held 2.60–2.64 GiB of memory at idle. Its Docker Compose guide recommends at least 4 CPU cores and 16 GiB RAM, with about 100 GiB of disk.

The TypeScript path is built on OpenTelemetry. You start the OTel Node SDK with LangfuseSpanProcessor, wrap the client with observeOpenAI, and wrap your own functions with observe:

This file adds 31 lines and removes 5, and installs four packages. We pinned the OTel Node SDK to 0.223.0, because @langfuse/otel 6.1.1 does not accept 0.300.0.

Langfuse successfully recreated the same trace tree, neatly tagging the spans as AGENT, GENERATION, and TOOL. It captured all the essentials: tool calls, tool definitions, and the complete message history. However, for the LLM output, it only saved the assistant's message—dropping the finish_reason, response ID, and the provider name.

We ran our deployment in Langfuse v4's events_only mode, which turns off the v1 trace endpoint. Because of this, the API didn't return a centralized trace object or root-level sums for tokens and costs, even though the UI calculated and displayed them perfectly (we didn't test other modes).

Costs showed up exactly as expected once we added a custom price entry. Since Langfuse calculates prices based on the specific usage types you define, and we only set rates for input and output, the separate reasoning tokens went unpriced. Finally, during our error test, the observe wrapper let the error bubble up to the agent, correctly flagging both the tool and the root span as an ERROR.

Phoenix self-hosts as two containers, one Python server and Postgres. In our measurement it held 0.47 GiB at idle. Phoenix is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0, so it is not open source. Authentication is off until you turn it on.

The TypeScript path uses Phoenix's register() helper and the OpenInference instrumentation for the OpenAI package. OpenInference is a set of OpenTelemetry attribute names for LLM spans. traceAgent and traceTool wrap the run and the tools:

This file adds 32 lines and removes 3, and installs three packages.

Phoenix rebuilt the same tree, typed as AGENT, LLM and TOOL. Each LLM span keeps the full OpenAI response object, plus the messages as flattened attributes. The root span stores no token count, but Phoenix computes a sum for the root and the trace when you read it. Cost and those sums are only in the GraphQL API and the UI, and the REST API has no per-trace endpoint.

Cost appeared after a custom price entry under Settings > Models, and Phoenix priced the reasoning tokens by falling back to the output price. In the error run, the tool span and the root were marked ERROR, and the tool span carried an exception event with the stack trace.

Opik self-hosts as eight containers, including ClickHouse, MySQL and ZooKeeper. In our measurement it held 3.69 GiB at idle, the most of the four. The self-hosted UI opened without a login, so every trace was readable from any machine that could reach the port.

The TypeScript path wraps the client with trackOpenAI and your own functions with track. By default trackOpenAI starts a new trace for every model call, so the file passes the run's span through the documented parent option:

This file adds 33 lines and removes 5. It installs opik-openai 2.2.142, and npm adds opik 1.11.14 as its peer, because opik-openai asks for opik ^1.8.61.

Opik successfully recreated the trace tree, and its trace object neatly tallies token counts across all LLM spans. In the logs, tool arguments are bundled into an array, and the LLM output only retains the assistant's message.

We did notice a quirk with the documented OpenAI wrapper (tested on the npm package opik 1.11.14): it tags model calls as general rather than llm, which incorrectly leaves the llm_span_count at zero. (We didn't test newer Opik core versions to see if this has changed). Additionally, because our synchronous tools execute in under a millisecond, they log the exact same start time as the subsequent LLM call, causing the UI to list the LLM call first out of order.

Cost tracking is entirely manual. Opik showed no costs by default, and the documentation doesn't mention a custom price table. We checked the configuration tabs on our 2.2.52 instance (Feedback definitions, AI Providers, Workspace preferences) and found no model pricing settings. To see costs, you have to manually assign a price to each individual span yourself—only the spans we hardcoded this way displayed a cost.

Finally, error reporting is highly detailed. If something fails, Opik attaches an error_info block—complete with the error type, message, and full traceback—directly to the tool span, the root span, and the overall trace.

AcruxCore self-hosts as five containers: Postgres, Redis, a Node API and worker, and nginx. In our measurement it held 0.39 GiB at idle, the least of the four. Its quickstart leaves sign-up open and ships a committed default GATEWAY_ENCRYPTION_KEY, which encrypts stored provider keys; replace it. We tested a local build from 2026-09-17.

The TypeScript path AcruxCore's docs put first is its gateway. The official openai client keeps working: you point its baseURL at ACRUXCORE_BASE_URL + "/gateway" and call a model registered in AcruxCore, which forwards each call to an OpenAI-compatible provider. The gateway records every model call as an llm span. The SDK's step helpers add the rest: traces.step opens the agent span, traces.wrap wraps each tool, and two headers file the gateway's spans under the agent span:

This file adds 30 lines and removes 5, and installs one package. It builds its own client, so it does not use provider.ts. The gateway refused our team API key, so the client uses a gateway virtual key created in the dashboard.

On this path every model call passes through the AcruxCore server, which none of the other four tools need. If you do not want a proxy in the request path, the SDK's register() helper sends OpenTelemetry spans from your process instead. On that path the step helpers do not join the openai package's spans, so you write the agent and tool spans by hand.

AcruxCore rebuilt the same tree, typed as agent, llm and tool, in call order. Each LLM span keeps the full response, the provider and the cached-token count, and the trace carries a token total. The LLM spans do not keep the tool definitions sent to the model, and no reasoning-token count was recorded. The trace took its name from the question, not from the agent span, and each LLM span is named by its start time.

Cost appeared on every LLM span and as a sum on the trace, from the custom price we set on the model in AcruxCore's model list. In the error run, the step helpers marked the tool span and the agent root as error with the error message, with no status code of ours. The API returned no stack trace.

All five tools accept traces over OTLP, the OpenTelemetry wire format. trace-otel.ts sends the same spans with no vendor package: the OTel Node SDK, the OTLP/HTTP protobuf exporter and the OpenInference OpenAI instrumentation. The exporter reads its endpoint and headers from environment variables:

We ran the two-tool question once per backend and changed only environment variables: the endpoint, the headers, and for Phoenix a resource attribute that sets the project name (without it, spans go to a default project). "Accepted" means the exporter reported success, which it does only for an HTTP 2xx, and we read the spans back through each API.

Opik stored the root and tool spans as general although AGENT and TOOL kinds were sent; the cause is Not tested. LangSmith mapped AGENT to its chain type. If you instrument with plain OTel and OpenInference attributes, your raw spans are not tied to one vendor, but span types, cost and trace views still differ by backend.

The first table covers setup: how much server each tool needs, how much code we changed in the agent, and how cost and the plain OTel exporter worked. Phoenix and AcruxCore had the smallest servers, and AcruxCore needed the fewest lines among the self-hosted tools. Opik was the only one without a price table.

The second table checks each trace against what LangSmith recorded for the same run, one field at a time. All five rebuilt the same tree with tokens and durations. They differ in span types, how much of the LLM output they keep, where token sums live, and how much detail they store for the failing tool.

Token totals for the two-tool question ranged from 1,910 to 2,111. Each tool traced a separate run and reasoning length varies, so these numbers do not compare the tools.

All five tools successfully traced our test agent, so the right choice really comes down to your team's specific constraints, infrastructure preferences, and how tracing fits into the rest of your MLOps tooling.

All four alternatives successfully recreated LangSmith’s trace tree. The real deciding factors are boilerplate code, span typing, cost tracking, and server bloat.

LangSmith remains the simplest option for LangChain users who can utilize the cloud. Otherwise, your choice depends on your priorities: Langfuse for community size, Phoenix for a lightweight Postgres footprint, Opik for strict Apache-2.0 compliance with deep error logging, or AcruxCore for combined tracing and tool governance on minimal hardware. Best of all, if you stick to standard OpenTelemetry spans, you aren't locked in—you can try them all and easily pivot later.

Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.), the chairperson of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, has said that he will issue a subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond to the committee’s request to meet with them on November 18 by Wednesday, November 11, according to ABC News. The House invited him to a “joint, closed-door briefing” with the heads of the House committees on China, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence, and that they will focus on his company’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage.”

Congress first called the embattled CEO on November 7, a few days after rumors started circulating about Huang’s “closeness” to a particular Chinese executive suspected of passing information to Chinese intelligence. The following day, Nvidia released a statement from Jensen admitting to an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, apologizing for his unfaithfulness, while the company’s board of directors confirmed it will launch an independent investigation regarding the allegations that the CEO has been specifically targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS). Aside from having to face Congress, Jensen Huang is also reportedly being looked into by the FBI.

It remains unclear whether Jensen Huang was targeted by intelligence agencies, but he came into prominence with the AI boom that was arguably fueled by Nvidia’s AI chips. This led to the AI race as we know it today, with the U.S. taking steps to delay China’s advancement for fears that it will use the technology for military purposes. We also don’t know if Huang Le or Alice Huang is actually a Chinese spy or an “innocent” bystander caught in a web of accusations. And, even if she did work with the MSS, the question remains as to whether she specifically targeted the Nvidia CEO or whether Chinese intelligence discovered their indiscretion and used that as a convenient tool for blackmail to extract information from her.

However, former CIA agent Darrel Blocker told ABC News that the authorities should just focus on Jensen. “I think that the biggest concern is that the focus or overfocus on just Jensen Huang and Nvidia risks losing sight of the fact that other people have been targeted by the Chinese. Are they talking to the engineers? Are they talking to other people who might have even more access than even the CEO has? So, this focus should not be singular; it should include everyone in the company, and quite frankly, every tech company out there should be looking at all the contacts that their officers and employees have.”

“It’s definitely not a one-time thing. When you run a trillion-dollar company, you know that you have a bullseye on your back; whether it’s from competition or rather from nation-states, so this is absolutely not a one-off. Jensen Huang is not the only person at Nvidia that has access to the crown jewels, so I would be looking at the other people in terms of the access that they enjoy and their proximity to Chinese nationals.”
